questions.q: An atom of element X has the electron configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴. Which ion does X form in its ionic compounds?
options: X²⁺
X⁶⁺
X²⁻
X⁶⁻
optionWhy: Gaining two electrons does give X a complete 3p sublevel, but electrons are negative: 16 protons and 18 electrons give a charge of 16 − 18 = −2, not +2.

Losing all six outer electrons would leave the full shell 1s² 2s² 2p⁶, but having a full shell does not make an ion form. Removing six electrons would need a very large amount of energy; a non-metal atom with a nearly complete outer sublevel gains two electrons instead.

X has six outer electrons (3s² 3p⁴). It gains two electrons, giving 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶, and with 16 protons and 18 electrons its charge is 2−. (X is sulfur, which forms S²⁻, as in sodium sulfide, Na₂S.)

The charge is not the number of outer electrons. X needs only two more electrons to complete its 3p sublevel, so it gains two and forms X²⁻ (the argon configuration). Gaining six electrons would carry it four electrons beyond the argon configuration.
questions.explain: X has six outer electrons (3s² 3p⁴). It gains two electrons, giving 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶, and with 16 protons and 18 electrons its charge is 2−. (X is sulfur, which forms S²⁻, as in sodium sulfide, Na₂S.)

questions.q: Which describes the ionic bonding in solid sodium chloride?
options: Attraction between oppositely charged ions in all directions
Transfer of one electron from each sodium atom to a chlorine atom
Attraction joining each Na⁺ to one Cl⁻ in an NaCl molecule
A pair of electrons shared unequally by Na and Cl atoms
optionWhy: The ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. It is non-directional: each Na⁺ ion attracts all the Cl⁻ ions around it in the lattice, and each Cl⁻ ion attracts all the Na⁺ ions around it.
Electron transfer is one way the ions can be formed, but it is an event, not the bond. The bond is the electrostatic attraction between the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions that exist in the lattice.
Sodium chloride contains no molecules. It is a giant lattice in which each Na⁺ ion is surrounded by, and attracted to, six Cl⁻ ions; NaCl gives the 1 : 1 ratio of the ions.
A shared electron pair is a covalent bond. In sodium chloride the electron has been transferred, and the particles are Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions held by electrostatic attraction.
questions.explain: The ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. It is non-directional: each Na⁺ ion attracts all the Cl⁻ ions around it in the lattice, and each Cl⁻ ion attracts all the Na⁺ ions around it.

questions.q: The formula of magnesium chloride is MgCl₂. What does this formula represent?
options: One molecule of one Mg atom bonded to two Cl atoms
Mg²⁺ ions combined 1 : 1 with chlorine molecules, Cl₂
A Mg atom sharing an electron pair with each Cl atom
The 1 : 2 ratio of Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in a lattice
optionWhy: Magnesium chloride contains no molecules. It is a lattice of Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in which each ion is surrounded by several ions of opposite charge; the formula gives only their ratio.
The subscript 2 counts chloride ions, not atoms in a Cl₂ molecule. The two Cl⁻ ions are separate, each surrounded by Mg²⁺ ions in the lattice.
Shared electron pairs are covalent bonds. Magnesium chloride is ionic: magnesium has lost two electrons to become Mg²⁺, and the ions are held by electrostatic attraction.
Ionic compounds exist as three-dimensional lattices, and their formulas are empirical formulas: MgCl₂ gives the simplest whole-number ratio of the ions, one Mg²⁺ for every two Cl⁻.
questions.explain: Ionic compounds exist as three-dimensional lattices, and their formulas are empirical formulas: MgCl₂ gives the simplest whole-number ratio of the ions, one Mg²⁺ for every two Cl⁻.

questions.q: What holds the hydrogen atom and the chlorine atom together in a molecule of hydrogen chloride, HCl?
options: The need of each atom to gain a full outer shell by sharing a pair of electrons
The shared pair of electrons itself, acting as a physical link between the atoms
The electrostatic attraction of both nuclei to a shared pair of electrons
The electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions H⁺ and Cl⁻
optionWhy: Sharing does give each atom a full outer shell, but a 'need' is not a force and cannot hold atoms together. The octet rule describes a tendency; the bond itself is the attraction between the shared pair and both nuclei.
The shared pair is not a rod or hook. It holds the atoms together only because both nuclei are electrostatically attracted to it; the bond is that attraction.
The shared pair lies between the H and Cl nuclei and is attracted to both of them. This electrostatic attraction holds the two atoms together, and it is what a covalent bond is.
HCl molecules contain no ions. The H–Cl bond is polar, with partial charges δ+ and δ−, but the electrons are shared. H⁺ and Cl⁻ form only when HCl reacts with water.
questions.explain: The shared pair lies between the H and Cl nuclei and is attracted to both of them. This electrostatic attraction holds the two atoms together, and it is what a covalent bond is.

questions.q: How does the carbon–carbon bond in ethyne, HC≡CH, compare with the carbon–carbon bond in ethane, CH₃CH₃?
options: It is longer and stronger
It is shorter and weaker
It is longer and weaker
It is shorter and stronger
optionWhy: The triple bond is stronger, but it is shorter, not longer. The extra shared electrons do not take up extra space between the atoms; they attract both nuclei and pull them closer together (120 pm against 154 pm).

The triple bond is shorter, but it is also stronger overall (839 against 346 kJ mol⁻¹). Alkynes react readily because addition breaks only part of the multiple bond: converting C≡C into C=C needs about 839 − 614 = 225 kJ mol⁻¹, less than a whole C–C bond. The C≡C bond as a whole is not weak.

The shared pairs do repel one another, but their attraction to both nuclei is the larger effect. The triple bond is shorter (120 pm) and stronger (839 kJ mol⁻¹) than the single bond (154 pm, 346 kJ mol⁻¹).

A triple bond has three shared pairs between the nuclei, against one in the single bond. More shared electrons attract both nuclei more strongly, pulling them closer (C≡C 120 pm, C–C 154 pm) and making the bond harder to break (839 against 346 kJ mol⁻¹).
questions.explain: A triple bond has three shared pairs between the nuclei, against one in the single bond. More shared electrons attract both nuclei more strongly, pulling them closer (C≡C 120 pm, C–C 154 pm) and making the bond harder to break (839 against 346 kJ mol⁻¹).

questions.q: In the vapour at lower temperatures, aluminium chloride exists as Al₂Cl₆ molecules, formed when two AlCl₃ units join through two bridging chlorine atoms. Which describes the new bonds that join the two units?
options: A lone pair on the aluminium atom of each unit is donated to a chlorine atom of the other unit
A lone pair on a chlorine atom of each unit is donated to the aluminium atom of the other
Al³⁺ ions in one unit attract Cl⁻ ions in the other unit, forming two ionic bonds
Each new bond forms from one electron of an aluminium atom and one of a chlorine atom
optionWhy: The aluminium atom in AlCl₃ has no lone pair: its three valence electrons are all in Al–Cl bonds. It is the acceptor. The donor is chlorine, which has three lone pairs.

In AlCl₃, aluminium uses all three valence electrons in bonds and has only six electrons, so it can accept a pair. A chlorine atom of the other unit has lone pairs and donates one, forming a coordination bond. Two such bonds join the units.
Aluminium chloride vapour consists of molecules, not ions: the Al–Cl bonds are covalent. The metal/non-metal rule for ionic bonding has exceptions, and aluminium chloride is one.

An aluminium atom in AlCl₃ has no unshared electron left to contribute, because all three of its valence electrons are already in Al–Cl bonds. Both electrons of each new bond must therefore come from chlorine.
questions.explain: In AlCl₃, aluminium uses all three valence electrons in bonds and has only six electrons, so it can accept a pair. A chlorine atom of the other unit has lone pairs and donates one, forming a coordination bond. Two such bonds join the units.

questions.q: Ammonia, NH₃, has three bonding pairs and one lone pair around the nitrogen atom. What is its molecular geometry?
options: Tetrahedral, as there are four electron domains around the nitrogen atom
Trigonal planar, as only the three bonding pairs repel one another
Flat, with 90° bond angles, as the atoms are drawn in its Lewis formula on paper
Trigonal pyramidal, as the lone pair occupies one of four tetrahedral domains
optionWhy: Tetrahedral is the electron-domain geometry, which includes the lone pair. The molecular geometry describes only the positions of the atoms, and with three H atoms around N it is trigonal pyramidal.

The lone pair is an electron domain and repels the bonding pairs strongly. Four domains around nitrogen give a tetrahedral arrangement, so the three H atoms are pushed below the N atom into a pyramid.
A Lewis formula is drawn flat and does not show angles. In three dimensions the four domains point to the corners of a tetrahedron, so NH₃ is trigonal pyramidal with angles of about 107°.

The four electron domains take up a tetrahedral arrangement (electron-domain geometry). Only three are occupied by atoms, so the atoms form a pyramid with N at the apex: trigonal pyramidal, with H–N–H angles of about 107°.
questions.explain: The four electron domains take up a tetrahedral arrangement (electron-domain geometry). Only three are occupied by atoms, so the atoms form a pyramid with N at the apex: trigonal pyramidal, with H–N–H angles of about 107°.

questions.q: Electronegativity values: H 2.2, C 2.6, O 3.4, F 4.0, P 2.2. Which bond is the most polar?
options: O–H
O–F
C–F
P–H
optionWhy: O–H is very polar (difference 3.4 − 2.2 = 1.2) and gives hydrogen bonding, but its difference is smaller than that of C–F (1.4). Polarity is set by the electronegativity difference, not by the ability to hydrogen bond.
O and F are the two most electronegative atoms here, but polarity depends on the difference: 4.0 − 3.4 = 0.6. Two strongly attracting atoms share the pair fairly evenly.
The electronegativity difference is 4.0 − 2.6 = 1.4, the largest of the four, so the shared pair is drawn most unequally, towards F.
P has many more protons than H, but electronegativity does not follow atomic number: both values are 2.2, so the difference is 0 and the bond is essentially non-polar.
questions.explain: The electronegativity difference is 4.0 − 2.6 = 1.4, the largest of the four, so the shared pair is drawn most unequally, towards F.

questions.q: Carbon dioxide, CO₂, has no net dipole moment (electronegativity: C 2.6, O 3.4). Which statement explains this?
options: Its two C=O bond dipoles are equal and point in opposite directions, so they cancel
Its C=O bonds are non-polar, as the electronegativity difference is below 1.8
It carries no overall charge, so no separation of charge can exist in the molecule
Its carbon atom has no lone pair, and only lone pairs can produce a net dipole
optionWhy: Each C=O bond is polar (difference 0.8, δ− on O). Carbon has two electron domains, so the molecule is linear and the two equal bond dipoles point in exactly opposite directions. Their vector sum is zero.
Any electronegativity difference makes a bond polar. A difference of 0.8 gives a clearly polar C=O bond; values near 1.8 are only a rough guide to where bonding becomes mainly ionic.
Many neutral molecules have a net dipole, for example H₂O. A dipole is a separation of partial charges within a neutral molecule. CO₂ has none because its bond dipoles cancel.

Lone pairs matter only through their effect on shape. A molecule without a lone pair on its central atom can still be polar (CH₃Cl). CO₂ is non-polar because it is linear and its equal bond dipoles cancel.
questions.explain: Each C=O bond is polar (difference 0.8, δ− on O). Carbon has two electron domains, so the molecule is linear and the two equal bond dipoles point in exactly opposite directions. Their vector sum is zero.

questions.q: Graphite conducts electricity. Which feature of its structure explains this?
options: It contains carbon ions that move through the layers when a voltage is applied
Its atoms are held by metallic bonding, as its shiny grey appearance suggests
Each carbon atom bonds to three others, leaving one electron per atom delocalized
Its layers slide over one another easily, carrying electric charge as they move
optionWhy: Graphite contains only covalently bonded carbon atoms, not ions. The mobile charged particles are delocalized electrons within each layer.

Graphite looks metallic but is a covalent network: each carbon atom is covalently bonded to three others. Its conduction comes from electrons delocalized within the covalent layers, not from metallic bonding.
In each layer every carbon atom forms three covalent bonds. Its fourth valence electron is delocalized across the layer, and these mobile electrons carry the current along the layers.
Sliding layers explain why graphite is soft and slippery; they are held only by weak London forces. Conduction comes from the delocalized electrons within each layer.
questions.explain: In each layer every carbon atom forms three covalent bonds. Its fourth valence electron is delocalized across the layer, and these mobile electrons carry the current along the layers.

questions.q: Liquid methanol, CH₃OH, contains hydrogen bonds. What is a hydrogen bond in methanol?
options: An attraction between the H of an O–H group and a lone pair on O in another molecule
The covalent bond between the O atom and the H atom within one methanol molecule
An attraction between the H atoms of one molecule and the H atoms of another
An attraction between an H atom of the CH₃ group and an O atom in a neighbouring molecule
optionWhy: A hydrogen bond forms when hydrogen, covalently bonded to an electronegative atom (here O), is attracted to a lone pair on an electronegative atom (O) of a neighbouring molecule.
That is a covalent bond inside the molecule. A hydrogen bond is an intermolecular attraction between the δ+ H of one molecule and an O atom of another.
Hydrogen atoms bonded to O are δ+, so two of them repel. A hydrogen bond links an H atom to an electronegative atom with a lone pair.
Only an H atom bonded to N, O or F takes part. The H atoms of the CH₃ group are bonded to carbon and are not δ+ enough to form hydrogen bonds.
questions.explain: A hydrogen bond forms when hydrogen, covalently bonded to an electronegative atom (here O), is attracted to a lone pair on an electronegative atom (O) of a neighbouring molecule.

questions.q: Ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH, mixes with water in all proportions, but hexane, C₆H₁₄, does not dissolve in water. Which statement explains this difference?
options: Ethanol splits into ions that water surrounds, but hexane does not form ions
Ethanol can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules, but hexane cannot
Hexane is less dense than water, so it floats on the water rather than dissolving
Hexane molecules are too large to fit into the gaps between water molecules
optionWhy: Ethanol dissolves as intact molecules; its solution does not conduct electricity. It dissolves because it forms hydrogen bonds with water, not because it ionizes.

The O–H group of ethanol forms hydrogen bonds with water, replacing the hydrogen bonds broken between water molecules. Hexane forms only London forces with water, far weaker than the hydrogen bonds it would have to break, so it does not dissolve.
Density decides which layer floats once two liquids fail to mix, not whether they mix. Ethanol is also less dense than water, yet it mixes completely.

Solubility depends on the attractions formed between solute and solvent, not on fitting into gaps. Sucrose molecules are larger than hexane molecules but dissolve readily because they hydrogen bond with water.
questions.explain: The O–H group of ethanol forms hydrogen bonds with water, replacing the hydrogen bonds broken between water molecules. Hexane forms only London forces with water, far weaker than the hydrogen bonds it would have to break, so it does not dissolve.

questions.q: In a paper chromatography experiment the baseline was drawn 1.0 cm above the bottom edge of the paper. At the end, the solvent front was 11.0 cm above the bottom edge and the centre of a spot was 4.4 cm above the bottom edge. What is the RF value of the spot?
optionWhy: This is 10.0 ÷ 3.4, the solvent distance divided by the spot distance. RF is the spot distance divided by the solvent distance, so it can never exceed 1.
This is 4.4 ÷ 11.0, with both distances measured from the bottom edge of the paper. The spot and solvent both started from the baseline, so measure from there: 3.4 ÷ 10.0 = 0.34.
This is (11.0 − 4.4) ÷ 10.0, the gap between the spot and the solvent front. Despite the name 'retardation factor', RF uses the distance the spot moved from the baseline: 3.4 ÷ 10.0 = 0.34.
Distance moved by the spot = 4.4 − 1.0 = 3.4 cm; distance moved by the solvent = 11.0 − 1.0 = 10.0 cm. RF = 3.4 ÷ 10.0 = 0.34.
questions.explain: Distance moved by the spot = 4.4 − 1.0 = 3.4 cm; distance moved by the solvent = 11.0 − 1.0 = 10.0 cm. RF = 3.4 ÷ 10.0 = 0.34.
questions.working: Distance moved by spot = 4.4 cm − 1.0 cm = 3.4 cm. Distance moved by solvent = 11.0 cm − 1.0 cm = 10.0 cm. RF = 3.4 cm ÷ 10.0 cm = 0.34 (no units).

questions.q: Which statement describes a metallic bond?
options: The sharing of electron pairs between each metal atom and its nearest neighbours
The electrostatic attraction between a lattice of cations and delocalized electrons
The attraction between cations and anions formed by electron transfer between metal atoms
The London forces acting between the closely packed atoms of a metal lattice
optionWhy: A student who pictures metallic bonds as localized bonds between neighbouring atoms, like covalent bonds, picks this. In a metal the valence electrons are delocalized over the whole lattice, not shared in pairs between two particular atoms.

This is the metallic bond as the IB defines it. Each atom releases its valence electrons into a delocalized system shared by the whole lattice, and the resulting cations are attracted to these electrons in all directions.
A student who models metallic bonding on ionic bonding picks this. A pure metal contains no anions: the negative charge is carried by delocalized electrons that belong to no particular atom.

A student who treats a metal like a molecular substance, held by intermolecular forces, picks this. A metal is a giant structure held by metallic bonding, the attraction between cations and delocalized electrons.
questions.explain: This is the metallic bond as the IB defines it. Each atom releases its valence electrons into a delocalized system shared by the whole lattice, and the resulting cations are attracted to these electrons in all directions.

questions.q: The melting points of the group 1 metals decrease down the group: lithium 180.5 °C, sodium 97.8 °C, potassium 63.4 °C. Which statement explains this trend?
options: Reactivity increases down the group, so the bonds break more easily when the metal is heated.
The cation radius increases, so the delocalized electrons are attracted less strongly.
Larger atoms form longer and weaker covalent bonds with each of their neighbouring atoms.
The cations and anions in the lattice get larger, so their ionic attraction weakens.
optionWhy: A student who treats one group 1 trend as the cause of another picks this. Reactivity and melting point are separate properties; both trends follow from the increasing radius, but reactivity does not cause the fall in melting point.

Every group 1 cation has a charge of +1, but the cation radius increases from Li⁺ to Na⁺ to K⁺. The delocalized electrons are further from the centre of positive charge, so the metallic bonding weakens and less energy is needed to melt the metal.

A student who pictures metallic bonds as localized bonds between pairs of atoms picks this. There are no covalent bonds in a metal; the attraction is between the cations and the delocalized electrons in all directions.

A student who models metallic bonding on ionic bonding picks this. A group 1 metal contains no anions: the lattice is of cations only, held by the delocalized electrons, and it is the increasing radius of these cations that weakens the attraction.
questions.explain: Every group 1 cation has a charge of +1, but the cation radius increases from Li⁺ to Na⁺ to K⁺. The delocalized electrons are further from the centre of positive charge, so the metallic bonding weakens and less energy is needed to melt the metal.

questions.q: Magnesium oxide (χ: Mg 1.3, O 3.4; Δχ = 2.1) lies high in the bonding triangle, towards the ionic vertex. Solid magnesium oxide does not conduct electricity, but molten magnesium oxide does. Which explanation is correct?
options: Melting splits its MgO molecules into separate ions, which then carry the current.
Its ions become liquid when it melts, and liquid ions can carry charge but solid ones cannot.
Its ions cannot move in the solid, but in the melt they move and carry the current.
Melting sets electrons free, which then move through the liquid and carry the current.
optionWhy: A student who pictures ionic compounds as made of molecules picks this. Solid MgO contains no molecules; it is already a lattice of Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions. Melting does not create ions, it lets the existing ions move.

A student who gives single particles the properties of the bulk material picks this. An ion is not solid or liquid; 'liquid' describes how the particles are arranged. In the melt the same ions are no longer held in fixed positions, so they can move.

High in the triangle, the ionic model applies: MgO is a lattice of Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions. In the solid the ions cannot move, so no current flows; when it melts the ions become mobile and carry the current.

A student who thinks current is always carried by electrons picks this. MgO has no delocalized electrons, solid or molten; in the melt the current is carried by Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions moving to the electrodes.
questions.explain: High in the triangle, the ionic model applies: MgO is a lattice of Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions. In the solid the ions cannot move, so no current flows; when it melts the ions become mobile and carry the current.

questions.q: The position of a binary compound in the bonding triangle is found from the electronegativities of its two elements. In the triangle the metallic vertex is at the bottom left, the covalent vertex at the bottom right and the ionic vertex at the top; the two bottom vertices are elements, for which Δχ = 0. For aluminium chloride, AlCl₃, χ(Al) = 1.6 and χ(Cl) = 3.2. What is the x-coordinate of AlCl₃ in the bonding triangle?
optionWhy: A student who averages over every atom in the formula gets (1.6 + 3 × 3.2)/4 = 2.8. The x-coordinate is the mean of the two elements' electronegativities, (1.6 + 3.2)/2 = 2.4; the number of chlorine atoms does not enter.
A student who adds the electronegativities without dividing by 2 gets 4.8. The x-coordinate is an average, (1.6 + 3.2)/2 = 2.4; 4.8 is off the scale, since no element has χ above 4.0.

A student who interchanges the axes gives Δχ = 3.2 − 1.6 = 1.6 as the x-coordinate. The bottom vertices have Δχ = 0, so Δχ (1.6) is the y-coordinate, which measures ionic character; the x-axis is the average electronegativity (2.4).

Both bottom vertices have Δχ = 0 and the ionic vertex at the top has the largest Δχ, so Δχ is the y-coordinate and x is the average electronegativity of the two elements: (1.6 + 3.2)/2 = 2.4. Each element is counted once, whatever the formula.
questions.explain: Both bottom vertices have Δχ = 0 and the ionic vertex at the top has the largest Δχ, so Δχ is the y-coordinate and x is the average electronegativity of the two elements: (1.6 + 3.2)/2 = 2.4. Each element is counted once, whatever the formula.
questions.working: The bottom edge (both bottom vertices) has Δχ = 0 and the ionic vertex at the top has the largest Δχ, so Δχ is the vertical (y) coordinate and the horizontal (x) coordinate is the average electronegativity. x = (χ(Al) + χ(Cl))/2 = (1.6 + 3.2)/2 = 2.4 (no units). The y-coordinate, Δχ = 3.2 − 1.6 = 1.6, is not asked.

questions.q: Which description of an alloy is correct?
options: A compound of a metal with other elements, bonded in a fixed ratio by formula
A mixture of a metal with other metals or non-metals, in variable amounts
A mixture of two or more metals, with no atoms of a non-metal present in it
A mixture of a metal with another element, made so that it is softer
optionWhy: A student who thinks the metals react to form a compound picks this. An alloy is a mixture with variable composition and no fixed formula; the atoms of the added element sit in the metallic lattice.

An alloy is a mixture, so its composition can vary, and the added element can be a metal (zinc in brass) or a non-metal (carbon in steel). Alloys usually have enhanced properties, such as greater hardness.
A student who learned the definition 'a mixture of metals' picks this. Alloys can contain non-metals: steel is iron with a small percentage of carbon.
A student who thinks mixing weakens a metal picks this. Alloys are usually harder and stronger than the pure metal, because the added atoms disrupt the layers so they slide less easily.
questions.explain: An alloy is a mixture, so its composition can vary, and the added element can be a metal (zinc in brass) or a non-metal (carbon in steel). Alloys usually have enhanced properties, such as greater hardness.

questions.q: Which statement about polymers is correct?
options: Polymers are synthetic plastics; substances made by living things are not.
Fats are natural polymers made of many glycerol and fatty acid units.
Glucose is a natural polymer, as it is the building block of starch and cellulose.
Cellulose (natural) and nylon (synthetic) are both polymers built from monomers.
optionWhy: A student who equates 'polymer' with 'plastic' picks this. Many polymers are natural: cellulose, starch, proteins, DNA and natural rubber are all macromolecules made of repeating monomer units.

A student who assumes every large biological molecule is a polymer picks this. A fat (triglyceride) contains one glycerol and three fatty acid units; it has no long chain of repeating units, so it is not a polymer.
A student who confuses monomer with polymer picks this. Glucose is the monomer; starch and cellulose are the polymers made from many glucose units.

Cellulose is a natural polymer of glucose, made by plants; nylon is a synthetic polyamide made industrially. Both are macromolecules built from many repeating monomer units, so being a polymer does not depend on being natural or synthetic.
questions.explain: Cellulose is a natural polymer of glucose, made by plants; nylon is a synthetic polyamide made industrially. Both are macromolecules built from many repeating monomer units, so being a polymer does not depend on being natural or synthetic.

questions.q: Propene, CH₂=CHCH₃, forms the addition polymer poly(propene), written as [repeating unit]ₙ. Which option gives the repeating unit and describes it correctly?
options: –CH₂=CH(CH₃)–, keeping each monomer's C=C
–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–, one unit of a single long chain
–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–, all three carbons in the main chain
CH₃CH₂CH₃, one of n separate small molecules
optionWhy: A student who thinks the monomer's double bond survives picks this. Polymerization happens because one bond of each C=C breaks; if the C=C remained, each carbon here would have five bonds.
One bond of each C=C breaks and the two former C=C carbons form the main chain, with CH₃ as a side group. The formula [–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–]ₙ represents one chain molecule containing n of these units.

A student who puts every carbon of the monomer into the chain picks this. Only the two C=C carbons form the main chain; the CH₃ group becomes a side group, so the chain has CH₃ branches on alternate carbons.

A student who reads n as a number of separate molecules writes the unit as a complete molecule, CH₃CH₂CH₃ (propane). The repeating unit has open bonds at both ends because each unit is covalently bonded to the next in one long chain, [–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–]ₙ; propane has no C=C and cannot polymerize.
questions.explain: One bond of each C=C breaks and the two former C=C carbons form the main chain, with CH₃ as a side group. The formula [–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–]ₙ represents one chain molecule containing n of these units.
